scenarios.title: Architecture diagram from the codebase
scenarios.prompt: Draw an architecture diagram of this project: its services, data stores, queues and external providers, and how they talk to each other.
scenarios.expected_output: One drawing with the four services (turnstile-gateway, keymaster-auth, ledger-orders, courier-worker), Postgres (shopapp-pg), Redis (token-cache), RabbitMQ (postbox-mq), and the external Paylode and Pigeonpost APIs, using the names from the code. Arrows are bound at both ends and follow the real calls: gateway to auth and orders, orders to Postgres, Paylode and the queue, the queue to the worker, the worker to Pigeonpost, auth to Postgres and Redis. No overlaps and every label fits.

scenarios.title: C4 container diagram
scenarios.prompt: Draw a C4 container diagram of this shop system for a new developer: the people who use it, the system boundary, each container with its technology, and the external systems it depends on.
scenarios.expected_output: A C4 container diagram: a Shopper person (ellipse or stick figure) outside a frame that marks the shopapp system boundary; inside it the containers turnstile-gateway, keymaster-auth, ledger-orders and courier-worker, the Postgres database shopapp-pg, the Redis token-cache and the RabbitMQ broker postbox-mq, each labelled with its technology (Node.js/TypeScript, Fastify, Postgres, Redis, RabbitMQ); Paylode and Pigeonpost outside the boundary as external systems. Arrows are bound and labelled with what flows, kept short.

scenarios.title: Request flow for placing an order
scenarios.prompt: Make a diagram of what happens when a user places an order, from the HTTP request hitting the gateway to the confirmation email going out. Show the steps in order, including the failure path when the card is declined.
scenarios.expected_output: A top-to-bottom flow or sequence diagram: turnstile-gateway checks the session with keymaster-auth (introspect), forwards POST /orders to ledger-orders, which inserts a pending order through OrderRepository into Postgres, charges through the Paylode client, marks the order paid (or payment_failed on decline), publishes order.placed to the order-events queue, and courier-worker sends the email through Pigeonpost. Names match the code.

scenarios.title: Update the diagram after a service is added
scenarios.prompt: I just added a service (see the latest commit). Update docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw so it matches the code again.
scenarios.expected_output: The existing diagram is edited in place: a new stockroom-inventory node with an arrow from ledger-orders (reserve stock) and to Postgres. Every existing element keeps its id (at least 80% of them, no full redraw) and nothing that still exists in the code is removed.

scenarios.title: /excalidraw:sync after a service is added
scenarios.prompt: /excalidraw:sync
scenarios.expected_output: The sync command finds the last commit (a new stockroom-inventory service) and updates docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw in place: a stockroom-inventory node with a code link to its source, an arrow from ledger-orders and one to Postgres, every existing id kept and the existing code links intact. It reports the code change and the edit it caused.

scenarios.title: Update the diagram and its code links after Redis is removed
scenarios.prompt: The code changed in the last commit. Bring docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw up to date, including the code links on its nodes.
scenarios.expected_output: Redis (token-cache) is gone from the diagram and keymaster-auth no longer points at it; sessions are now kept in memory inside keymaster-auth (a note or label is fine, a separate datastore box is not needed). Every node link points at a file that exists, so the link to redisTokenCache.ts is updated or removed. Other elements keep their ids.

scenarios.title: Update the diagram after a webhook endpoint is added
scenarios.prompt: We added a payment provider webhook in the latest commit. Update the architecture diagram in docs/diagrams/ to show it.
scenarios.expected_output: An arrow from Paylode back into the system (through turnstile-gateway or straight to ledger-orders) labelled as a webhook, and ideally the order.disputed event. Existing elements keep their ids.

scenarios.title: Add to a diagram the user has edited by hand
scenarios.prompt: Add the new stockroom-inventory service to docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw. I've been tidying that drawing by hand, so don't undo my changes.
scenarios.expected_output: stockroom-inventory is added with arrows from ledger-orders and to Postgres. The user's manual edits survive: token-cache stays where the user dragged it, ledger-orders keeps its red fill, and the user's free text note is untouched. No element is recreated.

scenarios.title: Readability review of a messy drawing
scenarios.prompt: Review docs/diagrams/checkout-sketch.excalidraw for readability and fix what's hard to read.
scenarios.expected_output: The overlapping boxes are moved apart, the free-floating arrows are bound to the boxes they point at, tiny text is enlarged to at least 14px, and labels fit their boxes. The five components and the note survive with their ids; nothing is recreated from scratch.

scenarios.title: Mermaid conversion
scenarios.prompt:
Turn this Mermaid into an Excalidraw drawing at docs/diagrams/checkout.excalidraw:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U((Shopper)) -->|HTTPS| G[turnstile-gateway]
  G -->|introspect| A[keymaster-auth]
  G -->|/orders| O[ledger-orders]
  O -->|charge| P[Paylode]
  O -->|order.placed| Q[(postbox-mq)]
  Q --> W[courier-worker]
  W -->|email| M[Pigeonpost]
```
scenarios.expected_output: Eight nodes with the Mermaid labels and seven arrows bound at both ends in the same directions, laid out left to right without overlaps.

scenarios.title: Architecture with nodes linked to code
scenarios.prompt: Draw the architecture of this project and link each component box to the source file that implements it, so clicking a box opens the code.
scenarios.expected_output: An architecture diagram like arch-overview where each service and client box carries a link (the element's link property) to a file that exists, e.g. ledger-orders to services/ledger-orders/src/server.ts or placeOrder.ts, Paylode to paylodeClient.ts, Postgres to packages/db/src/pool.ts.

scenarios.title: State diagram from a mentioned folder
scenarios.prompt: @services/ledger-orders/ Explain and diagram how an order's payment status changes.
scenarios.expected_output: A short explanation and a state diagram of an order's status with the status values from the code: pending (OrderRepository.insertPending) goes to paid (markPaid, when the Paylode charge succeeds) or to payment_failed (markPaymentFailed, when it is declined), directly or through a charge step. Arrows are bound and labelled with the trigger, and there are no statuses the code doesn't have.

scenarios.title: Discover the architecture, then draw containers
scenarios.prompt: Work out this project's architecture from its code and configuration before drawing anything, then draw a C4 container diagram at docs/diagrams/containers.excalidraw. Link every container and external system to the file that shows it exists.
scenarios.expected_output: Before drawing, a short model of the system: the four deployable services from the workspaces and docker-compose.yml, the Postgres, Redis and RabbitMQ containers, and the Paylode and Pigeonpost APIs found from their clients and env vars, with packages/db and packages/queue treated as libraries rather than containers. The drawing is a container diagram with a shopapp system boundary frame, each element named as in the code with its technology, arrows that follow the real calls (gateway to auth and orders, auth to Postgres and Redis, orders to Postgres, Paylode and the queue, the queue to the worker, the worker to Pigeonpost), and a code link on every container and external system to a file that exists.

scenarios.title: Component diagram scoped to one container
scenarios.prompt: Draw a C4 component diagram of ledger-orders at docs/diagrams/ledger-orders-components.excalidraw. Find the components from the code first.
scenarios.expected_output: A component diagram scoped to ledger-orders only: the Fastify server routes, placeOrder, OrderRepository, PaylodeClient and OrderEventsPublisher inside a ledger-orders boundary, with arrows from placeOrder to the repository, the Paylode client and the publisher, and those reaching shopapp-pg, the Paylode API and RabbitMQ outside the boundary. No internals of other services (UserRepository, RedisTokenCache, PigeonpostMailer, authMiddleware).

scenarios.title: Architecture review annotated on the drawing
scenarios.prompt: Review the architecture shown in docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw. What are the biggest risks? Mark them on the diagram.
scenarios.expected_output: Findings checked against the code and added as red notes with a severity, each pointing at its element: shopapp-pg (and the single RabbitMQ and Redis) as single points of failure, shopapp-pg shared by keymaster-auth and ledger-orders with a cross-service foreign key, courier-worker requeueing failed messages forever with no dead-letter queue or idempotency (duplicate emails, a poison message blocks the queue), markPaid then publish as a dual write with no outbox, the synchronous gateway, keymaster-auth and Paylode chain with no timeouts, and ledger-orders trusting x-user-id. Every original element keeps its id, position, size and colours; nothing is moved or redrawn.

scenarios.title: Security review of data crossing trust boundaries
scenarios.prompt: Do a security-focused review of the architecture in docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw: where does sensitive data or identity cross a trust boundary without enough protection? Annotate the diagram, but don't rearrange it.
scenarios.expected_output: Red severity notes added beside the affected elements: ledger-orders trusts the x-user-id header set by turnstile-gateway without verifying it, so anything that reaches it directly can act as any user; session tokens are checked by a call to keymaster-auth on every request; card payment details and the Paylode API key go to a third party; plain HTTP between services. The findings cite the files. Every original element keeps its id, position, size and colours.

scenarios.title: UML class diagram from a prompt alone
scenarios.prompt: draw me a uml class diagram for an online store
scenarios.expected_output: A UML class diagram (not boxes-and-arrows architecture) of an online store's domain: Customer, Order, Product and an order line (OrderItem/LineItem), optionally Cart, Payment, Address. Class boxes have name, attribute and operation compartments with visibility markers (+, -) and types. Relationships use UML notation: composition or aggregation diamonds at the whole (Order ◆ OrderItem), multiplicities (1, 0..*, 1..*), and inheritance or realisation with hollow triangles where used. Title names the diagram type.

scenarios.title: Vague 'UML diagram' request
scenarios.prompt: draw an e-commerce UML diagram
scenarios.expected_output: The assistant picks a sensible UML type for an unspecified request (a class diagram of the domain is the usual default; it says which type it chose and offers the others) and draws it with UML notation: class compartments with typed members, diamonds or triangles on relationships, multiplicities.

scenarios.title: UML use case diagram
scenarios.prompt: Draw a use case diagram for an ATM.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML use case diagram: actors (Customer, and the Bank or a technician) outside a labelled ATM system boundary; use cases as ellipses inside it (Withdraw Cash, Check Balance, Deposit, Transfer); associations as plain lines from actors to use cases; «include» (e.g. Authenticate/Enter PIN) and optionally «extend» as dashed arrows with the stereotype label.

scenarios.title: UML sequence diagram with an alternative
scenarios.prompt: Make a sequence diagram showing a user logging into a web app with a username and password, including the wrong-password case.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML sequence diagram with participants across the top (User, Browser/Frontend, Auth/API server, User DB), calls as solid arrows and replies dashed, and an alt fragment for valid vs invalid credentials (401 / error message).

scenarios.title: UML activity diagram
scenarios.prompt: Create an activity diagram for an online checkout process.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML activity diagram: an initial node, actions as rounded rectangles in order (review cart, enter shipping, enter payment, place order), at least one decision diamond with guard labels ([payment ok] / [declined]), a final node, and optionally a fork/join or swimlanes.

scenarios.title: UML state machine diagram
scenarios.prompt: Draw a state machine diagram for a door that can be opened, closed, locked and unlocked.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML state machine: states Opened, Closed, Locked as rounded boxes, an initial pseudostate, and transitions labelled with events (open, close, lock, unlock), optionally with guards. No transition from Locked straight to Opened.

scenarios.title: UML package diagram
scenarios.prompt: Draw a UML package diagram for a layered web application with presentation, business logic and data access layers.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML package diagram: packages (tabbed folders or labelled frames) for Presentation, Business Logic (Domain/Service) and Data Access (Persistence), each with a few example elements, and dashed dependency arrows (optionally «import») pointing downward from Presentation to Business to Data Access only.

scenarios.title: UML deployment diagram
scenarios.prompt: Draw a UML deployment diagram: a browser talks to a load balancer, which forwards to two app servers running the API, which use a PostgreSQL database server.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML deployment diagram: nodes with «device» or «executionEnvironment» stereotypes (client device with browser, load balancer, two app server nodes, database server), artifacts (api.jar or similar) deployed on the app servers, and communication paths labelled with protocols (HTTPS, TCP 5432).

scenarios.title: UML object diagram
scenarios.prompt: Draw a UML object diagram showing a snapshot: customer Alice with two orders, one of which contains a book.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML object diagram: instance boxes named instance:Class (alice:Customer, o1:Order, o2:Order, item:OrderItem/LineItem, book:Product) with attribute values (name = "Alice", status = …), joined by links (plain lines, no multiplicities).

scenarios.title: UML communication diagram
scenarios.prompt: Draw a UML communication diagram for placing an order between a customer, an order controller, an inventory service and a payment service.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML communication (collaboration) diagram: objects as boxes placed freely, links between them, and sequence-numbered messages along the links (1: placeOrder(), 1.1: reserveStock(), 1.2: charge(), 2: confirm).

scenarios.title: UML class diagram of real code
scenarios.prompt: Draw a UML class diagram of the ledger-orders service.
scenarios.expected_output: A UML class diagram of services/ledger-orders with its real types: OrderRepository (insertPending, markPaid, markPaymentFailed, findById), PaylodeClient (createCharge, refund), OrderEventsPublisher (orderPlaced), the Deps interface that aggregates the three, OrderRow and Charge. Members use the code's names and types; Deps → the three classes as associations/composition; each class links to its file.
